title: Console Playwright suite failed against a real API endpoint, only in the main checkout
description:
Found during final verification of the M10/M11 epics -- every individual
story's own review passed the full console Playwright suite in its isolated
worktree, but running the suite directly in the main checkout (the only place
\`.env.local\` actually exists, since it's gitignored and worktrees only
contain tracked files) surfaced 7-8 real failures.

Root cause: \`sites.spec.ts\`'s mock used a bare \`page.route('/sites', ...)\`
pattern. Playwright resolves a bare relative pattern against
\`playwright.config.ts\`'s \`baseURL\` (\`localhost:3000\`), so it only ever
matched requests to that origin. The moment \`.env.local\` sets
\`NEXT_PUBLIC_AURITUS_API_ENDPOINT\` to a real deployed API (as it does on
this machine, per \`AGENTS.local.md\`), \`fetchSites()\`'s real request target
no longer matches the mock, goes out live and unmocked, and the test
observes a genuine 401 from the real backend. Every other spec file in
\`console/tests/\` already uses a \`**\`-prefixed glob for exactly this reason
-- \`sites.spec.ts\` was the one file that didn't.

A separate, unrelated flake was also found and fixed in the same pass:
\`costs.spec.ts\`'s site-filter test asserted against a \`requestedUrls\` array
populated by an independent route-handler listener with no ordering
guarantee relative to a \`waitForRequest\` call already used in the same
test -- fixed to assert directly on the object \`waitForRequest\` returns.

Fixed directly on \`fix/console-test-origin-and-flakiness\`, merged to
develop. Confirmed stable across 6 consecutive full-suite runs (25/25) after
the fix, including 2 runs after the merge landed on develop itself.

## Lesson for future review discipline

Every worktree-based review in this session ran the console suite in an
environment that happened to differ from the real dev machine in a way that
masked this bug. A final sanity pass on the actual integration branch (not
just each feature branch in isolation) is what caught it -- worth doing
routinely at the end of a batch of merges, not only as an afterthought.
